# Nanobodies targeting EGFR provide insight into conformations stabilized by glioblastoma mutations

**Authors:** Sean M Watson; Edward P Harvey; Novalia Pishesha; Hidde L Ploegh; Timothy A Springer

**Affiliations:** 1Program in Cellular and Molecular Medicine, Department of Pediatrics, Boston Children’s Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 2Department of Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology, Harvard Medical School, , Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 3Department of Immunology and Infectious Diseases, Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 4Division of Immunology, Boston Children’s Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 5Department of Pediatrics, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

Oncogenic mutations in the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) promote tumorigenesis by stabilizing active or pre-active receptor conformations. Most EGFR-driven cancers are characterized by kinase domain mutations that directly activate the receptor. However, brain cancers such as glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) uniquely harbor mutations in the EGFR ectodomain that allosterically activate the kinase domain. Despite significant advances in understanding the physiological and pathogenic roles of EGFR, the conformational characteristics that define ligand-independent EGFR activation in GBM remain poorly understood. In this study, we use naive and post-immune yeast-displayed nanobody libraries to discover four nanobody groups that with benchmark nanobodies define a total of five groups with unique binding signatures and specificities for GBM mutation-stabilized conformational states. Nanobodies in Groups 1 and 2 block ligand, selectively bind the inactive, tethered conformation, and favor wild-type EGFR over GBM-stabilized conformations. In contrast, nanobodies in Groups 4 and 5 do not block ligand, target active or pre-active conformations, and selectively bind GBM-stabilized conformations. Additionally, nanobodies in Group 3 block ligand and appear to be conformation agnostic. We observed domain-specific bias in the nanobodies' selectivity for GBM mutations, suggesting that mutations across different ectodomain regions stabilize distinct conformations. This work advances our understanding of EGFR conformational equilibria in the context of GBM. The observed cooperativity and mutation-dependent binding of nanobodies emphasize their utility in dissecting EGFR activation mechanisms and in developing targeted therapies for EGFR-driven cancers, including GBM.

Keywords: single-domain antibody (sdAb, nanobody); epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR); receptor tyrosine kinase; protein conformation; glioblastoma

Conformation-selective mAbs or nanobodies—the variable domain of heavy chain only antibodies (VHH) found in camelids (1)—can be used to selectively bind and stabilize active and inactive conformational states of membrane proteins, such as integrins (2, 3, 4) and G-protein coupled receptors (5, 6, 7, 8). For the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), high-resolution structures exist for the tethered, monomeric state—many of which are complexed with mAb or nanobody—and the ligand-bound, dimeric state (Fig. 1, A and B). However, emerging evidence suggests the existence of additional physiologically relevant EGFR conformations, including unliganded homodimers and oligomers (9, 10, 11, 12, 13). The current paucity of conformation-selective mAbs targeting active or pre-active EGFR may be attributed to the focus on developing therapeutic mAbs, which has led to an abundance of antibodies that block ligand binding and stabilize the inactive, tethered conformation (14, 15, 16). mAbs that bind active or pre-active conformations might be thought to have minimal therapeutic value, as stabilizing the receptor in the active conformation would likely drive oncogenicity in vivo. However, recent advances in antibody-drug conjugates (17) and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapies (18) provide opportunities to develop mAbs that selectively target and eliminate cells expressing aberrantly activated EGFR in pathological contexts. Despite the broad clinical success of anti-EGFR therapies in various cancers, there are no FDA-approved EGFR-targeting drugs for GBM, a highly aggressive brain cancer characterized by frequent EGFR mutations and poor prognosis (19, 20, 21).

*Figure 1: GBM mutations cluster in the domain I-II interface or the domain II-IV interface. The most frequently mutated residues in GBM, R84, A265, and G574, are shown with yellow C alpha spheres (A and B). Disulfides are shown as orange sticks. A, crystal structure of the tethered EGFR monomer (PDB: 1YY9 (60)). B, crystal structure of the ligand-bound homodimer (PDB: 3NJP (50)). C, crystal structure of the variant III (vIII) glioblastoma deletion mutant that is missing most of domain I and domain II due to an exon 2 to 7 deletion (PDB: 8UKV (46)).*

The EGFR ectodomain comprises four domains that adopt distinct orientations in the inactive and active states. Domains I and III are globular and come together to bind EGF between them in the ligand-bound dimeric state (Fig. 1B). In contrast, domains II and IV are elongated and rich in disulfide bonds. An intramolecular tether extends from domain II and binds across domain IV, stabilizing the closed or tethered monomeric conformation (Fig. 1A), which allosterically stabilizes the kinase domain in its inactive conformation (22). Thermodynamic characterization of the domain II-IV interface suggests that 80 to 97% of cell-surface EGFR adopts a tethered conformation (23). Oncogenic mutations stabilize the active KD conformation in the absence of ligand, shifting the cell-surface equilibrium towards the active state and driving tumorigenesis (24, 25).

In most EGFR-driven cancers, EGFR mutations occur in the kinase domain. In GBM, the vast majority of tumorigenic EGFR mutations are in the ectodomain, which likely contributes to the poor clinical efficacy of kinase inhibitors in GBM compared to other cancer types (19, 20, 21). The most prevalent GBM mutation is variant III (vIII), which is missing most of domains I and II due to an exon 2 to 7 deletion (Fig. 1C). This drives oncogenicity by stabilizing constitutively active homodimers that are resistant to internalization (26, 27, 28). Point mutations in GBM cluster spatially in the domain I-II and domain II-IV interfaces (Fig. 1, A and B). Ligand-bound crystal structures of the most common domain I-II mutants, R84 K and A265 V, suggest they stabilize a pre-active conformation by breaking autoinhibitory interactions in the domain I-II interface (29). This pre-active state is further supported by the finding that R84 K and A265 V increase affinity for ligand (29, 30).

In this work, we utilize libraries of nanobodies displayed on the surface of yeast cells (31) to identify nanobodies that selectively target active EGFR conformations. We discovered conformation-selective nanobodies that we propose stabilize mutually exclusive conformations, either active or inactive. Two groups of nanobodies that stabilize an active conformation selectively bind GBM mutants over WT while two groups of nanobodies that stabilize the inactive conformation selectively bind WT over GBM mutants. An additional group of nanobodies is directly competitive with ligand and appears to be conformation agnostic.

## Results and discussion

### Discovery of conformation-selective nanobodies

To select nanobodies from yeast-displayed libraries, we generated soluble EGFR antigen and enriched the nanobody libraries for binders to this antigen (Figs. 2 and 3). To stabilize soluble EGFR homodimers in active-like conformations, we generated Fc fusion constructs ((sEGFR)2-Fc) comprising the EGFR ectodomain C-terminally fused to the human IgG1 Fc (Fig. 2C). We reasoned the EGFR homodimer would adopt active-like conformations by stabilizing the ectodomain conformation that is allosterically coupled to kinase-active EGFR on the cell surface (32) by forcing close association of monomers and creating steric hindrance between them, thereby destabilizing the domain II-IV tether.

*Figure 2: Soluble EGFR used as antigen in yeast-displayed nanobody selections. A, dimerization of cell-surface EGFR by ligand is allosterically transmitted to the kinase domains, which form an asymmetric dimer, with one active monomer that can trans-phosphorylate tyrosines in the C-terminal tail. B, the sEGFR Fc-fusion monomer (sEGFR-Fc) and ∗C) the Fc-fusion homodimer ((sEGFR)2-Fc) were cleaved with IdeS protease, yielding the EGFR ectodomain molecularly fused to the Fc hinge. D, gel filtration before and after IdeS cleavage. left: Gel filtration on an S200 column shows the (sEGFR)2-Fc elutes as a single monodisperse peak before and after ideS cleavage. Right: The sEGFR-Fc was generated by co-transfecting plasmids containing EGFR Fc-fusion and Fc. This yielded three separate species (sEGFR)2-Fc, sEGFR-Fc, and Fc (Fig. S1), which were separated by gel filtration using two S200 columns in series. E, isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) experiments demonstrate (sEGFR)2-Fc binds EGF with a Kd of 12 ± 1.1 nM, has N value of 0.73 ± 0.0016 Sites, ΔH of 23,000 ± 89 cal/mol, and ΔS of 115 cal/mol/deg.*

*Figure 3: Enrichment of yeast libraries for nanobodies binding to (sEGFR)2-hinge. A, yeast cells expressing a library of nanobodies were incubated with positive and negative selection antigens. Yeast cells expressing nanobodies binding to positive selection antigen were kept for future rounds of sorting while those not binding to antigen or binding to negative selection antigen were removed from the library. B, yeast displayed nanobody libraries were depleted for binders to sEGFR-hinge and enriched for binders to (sEGFR)2-hinge in the absence (left) or presence (right) of EGF ligand through one MACS and three rounds of FACS. Decreasing concentrations of ligand were used to enrich for high affinity binders. This sorting strategy is representative of two of three selections in which kinetic selection was done (Table S1).*

Using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC), we confirmed that (sEGFR)2-Fc has affinity for EGF ligand near that of cell-surface EGFR (Fig. 2E), which aligns with previous literature (33). After purifying (sEGFR)2-Fc, we cleaved the Fc region below the hinge using IdeS protease (Fig. 2, C and D, left); the Fc was removed to prevent enriching the nanobody libraries for Fc-binders. The resultant soluble EGFR homodimer (sEGFR)2-hinge comprises the EGFR ectodomain attached to 15 residues of the Fc hinge, including the hinge disulfides, which maintain dimerization. To increase the likelihood that the enriched nanobodies are selective for active EGFR, we depleted the libraries for binders to inactive, monomeric EGFR. To this end, we generated soluble EGFR monomers (sEGFR-hinge, Figs. 2B, S1).

To maximize our odds of discovering diverse nanobodies selective for active EGFR conformations, we performed three separate selection campaigns (Table S1). The first and second selection campaigns were performed with a synthetic (naive) library of 2 x 109 unique nanobody clones (34). For the third selection campaign, we generated a post-immune nanobody library after immunizing an alpaca with (sEGFR)2-hinge, among other antigens. This library contained an estimated 2 x 108 yeast transformants, although molecular diversity was likely much lower, as it was limited by the number of heavy-chain-antibody-expressing B cells from alpaca peripheral blood used to make the cDNA library with which yeast was transformed. Our first selection campaign yielded low-affinity nanobodies (Table S1). In response, we used kinetic selections in our second and third campaigns (35). Kinetic selections enrich nanobody binders with slow off rates, thereby increasing the likelihood of discovering high-affinity nanobodies.

We used magnetic-activated cell sorting (MACS) and multiple rounds of fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS) (Fig. 3). Using two strategies in parallel, we enriched for binders to (sEGFR)2-hinge with and without EGF. We suspected that both EGF-bound and unliganded (sEGFR)2-hinge conformations might resemble oncogenic EGFR conformations that couple to active kinase dimer conformations. By depleting the library for nanobody binders to sEGFR-hinge, we simultaneously removed nanobodies selective for the inactive EGFR conformation and the Fc hinge. Depletion with sEGFR-hinge was only performed in selections in absence of ligand, as addition of ligand drives soluble EGFR monomers to form homodimers (29, 36, 37). Libraries were additionally depleted with detergent solubilized Spodoptera frugiperda (Sf9) insect cell membranes to remove polyreactive nanobodies binding to multiple antigens.

Following the third round of FACS, Illumina sequencing of VHH in each successive selection round elucidated enrichment of nanobody sequences. In parallel to Illumina sequencing, we isolated individual yeast clones from the enriched nanobody libraries and tested their binding to (sEGFR)2-hinge using analytical flow cytometry. Nanobody clones identified by either method were expressed and purified as soluble nanobodies for further characterization.

### Specificity and affinity of nanobodies for the cell surface EGFR

In total, we expressed and purified 59 unique nanobodies (HD01-HD59) that contain C-terminal V5 and His tags. ‘HD’ denotes discovery in selections for EGFR Hinge Dimer ((sEGFR)2-hinge). Of 59 nanobodies, 56 were biochemically tractable and tested for binding to cell-surface EGFR using indirect immunofluorescence staining. Initially, each nanobody was used to stain cell-surface EGFR at single concentrations of 5 to 10 μM. In all, 21 out of 56 (38%) nanobodies showed greater than twofold binding to EGFR over background. Titration on EGFR transfectants yielded preliminary EC50 values (Table S1). Of the 21 nanobodies (Table S2), six had EC50 values of less than 500 nM and were chosen for further characterization (Fig. 4). These six nanobodies show variable maximum mean fluorescence intensity (MFI), which may relate to differences in off-rates. Washing was performed after primary and secondary staining; faster off rates result in more dissociation during wash steps, resulting in lower MFIs.

*Figure 4: Titrations of HD nanobodies and benchmark nanobodies. A, nanobodies were incubated with Ba/F3 WT EGFR stable transfectants for 50 min at room temperature, moved to 4 °C for 10 min, washed, and stained with Alexa Fluor 647-labeled anti V5 and subjected to immunofluorescent flow cytometry. Measurements were performed in triplicate on three separate days. B, results from A. The two single-digit nanomolar binders (HD25 and HD57) were discovered in kinetic selections to enrich for nanobodies with slow off rates (Table S1).*

To bridge our work to the broader community of anti-EGFR nanobodies with known epitopes, we searched the Protein Data Bank (PDB) for structures containing nanobody-bound EGFR. Four such benchmark nanobodies (38, 39, 40) were characterized alongside the HD nanobodies. 7D12 binds domain III, is directly competitive with the ligand, and is likely not conformationally selective (38). EgA1 and 9G8 bind overlapping epitopes in domain III, are allosterically competitive with ligand, and stabilize an inactive conformation (38). G10 has been reported to selectively bind the ligand-bound conformation (39). Benchmark nanobodies were discovered after alpaca immunizations, and their high affinities are likely due to affinity maturation in vivo (41). In contrast, nanobodies discovered in naive libraries are often low-affinity, as they have not been affinity-matured. We also included two benchmark mAbs. LA22 is not conformation-specific and is competitive with EGF for binding to domain III (42). mAb 806 was selected for binding to the vIII mutant (43). mAb 806 binds an epitope that is exposed in oncogenic GBM mutations (9) and active or preactive forms of the receptor (44, 45). While preparing this manuscript, a structure of a vIII-selective nanobody was published (46).

## Cell-surface antibody binning reveals HD nanobodies bind four distinct epitopes

To map the relationship between antibody epitopes, we performed competition binding assays on cell-surface EGFR using co-incubated binders which included EGF. Cells were co-incubated with (1) a CF647-labeled binder at its EC50 concentration (Fig. 5A and x axis axis) and (2) an unlabeled competitor at 100x its EC50 (Fig. 5A, y axis). After 3 to 4 h at 4 °C, the MFI of the labeled binder was measured by flow cytometry. Competition (or negative cooperativity) results in a decrease in MFI compared to the no-competitor control while positive cooperativity results in an increase in MFI. If the two binders are directly competitive and have identical binding kinetics, ∼99% of the labeled binder is expected to be competed off based on the use of the competitor at 100x its EC50.

*Figure 5: HD nanobodies recognize at least four distinct epitopes. A, competition between fluorescently labeled and unlabeled nanobodies, antibodies, and EGF for binding to Ba/F3 stable EGFR-transfectants. The ratio of specific mean fluorescent intensity (sMFI) in flow cytometry in presence and absence of competitor ± S.D. represent competition for the same epitope or negative cooperativity (red), no competition (white), or positive cooperativity (blue). Binders are clustered on the x and y axes according to results in (B) and binding domains in EGFR are also labeled on the y axis. B, Hierarchical clustering shows that HD nanobodies recognize at least four distinct epitopes. C, a community network plot illustrates competition or negative cooperativity between antibodies. Gray lines between antibody nodes indicate unidirectional competition and black lines indicate reciprocal competition. D, Summary of results. E, crystal structures of nanobodies 7D12 (PDB: 4KRL), EgA1 (PDB: 4KRO), and EgB4 (PDB: 7OM4) binding EGFR were superimposed onto the tethered EGFR monomer structure (PDB: 1YY9). Nanobodies are shown as transparent surfaces and colored according to their cluster colors. Domains in EGFR shown as cartoon are blue (I), green (II), orange (III), and red (IV).*

Hierarchical clustering of cooperativity (47) suggests that the HD nanobodies define at least four epitopes and benchmark nanobodies define at least one more (Fig. 5B). A community network algorithm (48) that only considered inhibition and not positive cooperativity independently identified the same groups (Fig. 5C). Distinct groups are formed by HD26, HD55, and HD57 (green); G10, EgA1, and 9G8 (yellow); HD25, 7D12, and LA22 (blue-green); EgB4 and HD30 (orange); and HD01 is the single member of yet another group (magenta). For members of the same group that exhibit negative cooperativity, the simplest interpretation is that they bind overlapping epitopes and therefore are directly competitive; however, we cannot rule out that they stabilize mutually exclusive conformations and are therefore allosterically competitive. By comparing HD nanobodies to benchmark nanobodies/mAbs with known epitopes or conformational selectivity, we can develop insight as to which nanobodies share similar binding epitopes or stabilize similar conformations (Fig. 5D).

Group 2 comprises nanobodies EgA1, 9G8, and G10. Crystal structures of EgA1 and 9G8 bound to tethered, monomeric EGFR (EgA1 is in Fig. 5E) show that they bind overlapping epitopes in domain III and allosterically stabilize the tethered conformation by sterically occluding the open, ligand-bound conformation (38). In agreement, Group 2 nanobodies are reciprocally competitive with one another and EGF. G10 was originally reported to selectively bind ligand-bound EGFR (39); however, this discrepancy might result from our reconstruction of G10 nanobody (Table S2) from its reported CDR sequences only, in the absence of knowledge of its framework sequence.

Group 1 nanobodies (HD26, HD55, and HD57) are cooperative with Group 2 nanobodies (Fig. 5D), suggesting they also stabilize the tethered conformation. Further supporting the conclusion that Group 1 and Group 2 nanobodies bind the inactive, tethered conformation, they compete with EGF, which stabilizes the active conformation, and compete with mAb 806, which stabilizes a pre-active or intermediate conformation. Because they do not compete with one another, Group 1 and Group 2 nanobodies must bind to different regions of EGFR. Taken together, the results suggest that Group 1 and Group 2 nanobodies bind to distinct epitopes and cooperate by stabilizing the tethered, monomeric EGFR conformation.

Group 3 antibodies include HD25, 7D12, and mAb LA22. The latter two antibodies bind overlapping epitopes in domain III and block EGF binding. Crystal structures and epitope mapping experiments suggest they are not conformation-specific (38, 42) (7D12 is in Fig. 5E); HD25 thus likely has similar attributes. HD25 is strongly competitive with 7D12 but minimally competitive with LA22, indicating an overlapping epitope with 7D12 but not LA22.

Group 4 nanobodies comprise HD30 and EgB4. The EgB4 epitope spans the domain I-II interface (EgB4 is in Fig. 5E). Interestingly, HD30 and EgB4 show cooperativity with ligand (Fig. 5A), suggesting that they have selectivity for an active or pre-active conformation. This is further supported by their cooperativity with mAb 806, which is known to recognize a pre-active conformation that is intermediate between the tethered and ligand-bound conformation.

Group 5 comprises the single nanobody HD01, which is allosterically cooperative with EGF, HD30, EgB4, and mAb 806. Taken together, this suggests that HD01 binds a novel epitope and stabilizes an active or pre-active conformation. Although mAb 806 is specific for a pre-active conformation, it is allosterically competitive with EGF ligand as its epitope is sterically blocked by the neighboring receptor in the ligand-bound homodimer (45).

### Domain I-II GBM mutations stabilize a distinct conformation from domain IV and vIII mutations

We next probed nanobody selectivity for common GBM mutants (Fig. 6). GBM mutations are hypothesized to change the conformational ensemble of cell-surface EGFR. These mutations activate the receptor in the absence of ligand and increase apparent ligand-binding affinity, indicating they stabilize an intermediate or preactive conformation (9, 24, 29, 30). Because the nanobodies were raised against WT EGFR, their selectivity for or against GBM mutants likely reports on the conformation(s) stabilized by the mutations. Taken together, nanobodies that bind WT over GBM mutants likely stabilize the inactive/tethered conformation, while those that bind GBM mutants over WT likely stabilize an intermediate or preactive conformation.

*Figure 6: Nanobody selectivity elucidates distinct conformational states stabilized by GBM mutations. A, single concentration measurements of antibodies binding to oncogenic EGFR mutants on the cell surface show distinct binding characteristics. Measurements were performed in triplicate at WT EC50 concentrations. Values are normalized to expression (LA22 binding) and to WT binding. Asterisks indicate statistically significant binding compared to WT, determined using unpaired t-tests with Bonferroni correction, p-value: ∗, < 0.0125; ∗∗, < 0.00125. Error bars show S.D. B, cell-surface antibody titrations on oncogenic mutants further demonstrate the distinct characteristics shown in A. Values are normalized to expression (LA22 binding). All measurements were performed on transiently transfected Expi293 F cells expressing either WT EGFR or GBM mutations.*

As an initial test, we measured nanobody binding to a panel of oncogenic GBM mutants at a single concentration (Fig. 6A). We used the WT EC50 concentration of each nanobody to give the most sensitivity to an increase or decrease in binding. We saw a significant decrease in HD26, HD55, and HD57 binding to vIII and the domain IV point mutation, G574V, compared to WT. In agreement, competition assays suggest these Group 1 nanobodies are selective for an inactive state (Fig. 5), which implies they target an inactive conformation stabilized in the WT receptor and destabilized by GBM mutations. Furthermore, the Group 5 nanobody HD01 selectively binds vIII and G574 V over WT (Fig. 6A). Taken together, these results suggest that vIII and G574 V stabilize a shared conformation recognized by HD01 that is destabilized by Group 1 nanobodies.

Interestingly, the selectivity of HD01 (Group 5) and Group 1 nanobodies for the domain I and II mutants R84 K and A265 V is decreased in magnitude compared to their selectivity for vIII and G574 V. In comparison to vIII and G574 V, HD01 binds domain I-II mutants only modestly better than WT. In contrast, Group 1 nanobodies fail to bind vIII and G574 V yet show only a modest decrease in binding to domain I-II mutants. In a further contrast, mAb 806 selectively binds the two most common domain I-II mutants, R84 K and 265V, with high affinity, but shows only modest selectivity for G574V. These findings suggest that the domain I-II and domain IV mutants stabilize distinct conformations.

The WT-selective Group 1 nanobodies, HD26, HD55, and HD57, show a >100-fold decrease in apparent affinity for vIII and G574V compared to WT (Fig. 6B). The >100-fold decrease in apparent affinity suggests that the WT receptor adopts the Group-1 targeted inactive conformation 100x more frequently than the vIII and G574 V mutants.

The Group 4 nanobodies HD30 and EgB4 fail to bind vIII (Fig. 6A), in agreement with cross-competition results showing they bind similar epitopes (Fig. 5) and structural evidence that the EgB4 epitope includes residues in both domains I and II, which are missing in vIII (Fig. 1C) (40). Nonetheless, the two nanobodies exhibit distinct responses to GBM mutations. HD30 shows no binding preference for domain I and II GBM mutants but demonstrates increased binding to the domain IV mutant. EgB4 exhibits reduced binding to the domain I-II R84 K and A265 V mutants, which are in the interface between domains I and II (Fig. 1). The epitope to which EgB4 binds has identical conformations in EGF-bound dimeric and tethered monomeric structures (40). Therefore, the decreased binding of EgB4 to the R84K and A265V mutants appears attributable to structural perturbations in this interface caused by the mutations. In contrast to EgB4, HD30 shows a preference for the domain IV mutant. Lack of effect of Domain I-II mutants on HD30 binding would be explained if unlike EGB4, its epitope is localized exclusively within Domain I or Domain II and not to their inteface.

EGF binding to EGFR allosterically stabilizes the active kinase domain conformation through “outside-in” signaling. Reciprocally, in "inside-out" signaling, stabilizing the kinase domain in the active conformation with the tyrosine kinase inhibitor gefitinib stabilizes the ectodomain in active or pre-active conformations (32, 49). We tested nanobody binding to inside-out stabilized conformations using gefitinib to bind to and stabilize the active kinase domain conformation and lapatinib to stabilize the inactive conformation (Fig. S4). None of the nanobodies tested showed selectivity for EGFR conformations stabilized by either inhibitor compared to control. This indicates either that inside-out signaling was too weak to be measurable in our assays or that it stabilizes a conformation distinct from that recognized by the HD nanobodies.

## Conclusions

In this work, we discovered and characterized a suite of anti-EGFR nanobodies. EC50s for cell-surface EGFR ranged from single-digit nanomolar to several hundred micromolar (Table S1). The first selection campaign (HD01-HD24) was performed without kinetic selections, and the median affinity of the EGFR-specific nanobodies was 72 μM (Table S1). Our second selection campaign (HD25-HD55) used the same synthetic library and included kinetic selections; the resultant median affinity was 700 nM for all EGFR-specific nanobodies, a ∼100-fold increase in median affinity. Our third selection campaign (HD56-HD59) utilized a post-immune library and yielded our highest affinity nanobody, HD57 (∼2 nM EC50). However, the most conformation-specific nanobody identified here, HD01, has an affinity of 500 nM and was identified in the screen without kinetic selection.

Figure 7 summarizes HD nanobody binding preferences and deduced epitopes. Nanobody Groups 1, 2, and 3 are all competitive with EGF ligand, indicating either that their epitopes overlap with the ligand-binding residues (directly competitive) or that they stabilize a conformation that is mutually exclusive from the ligand-bound, open conformation (allosterically or indirectly competitive). Epitope mapping and previous crystal structures showed that Group 3 antibodies LA22 and 7D12 are directly competitive with the EGF ligand. In contrast, structures of EGFR-bound Group 2 nanobodies, 9G8 and EgA1, show that they are allosterically or indirectly competitive with ligand and stabilize the tethered conformation. Cooperativity between Group 2 and Group 1—comprising HD26, HD55, and HD57—suggests that Group 1 nanobodies also stabilize the tethered conformation. Group 1 preference for WT over vIII and G574 V also aligns with our model that they stabilize the tethered conformation. In summary, Group 3 antibodies directly compete with EGF while Group 1 and 2 nanobodies bind distinct epitopes, are cooperative with one another, and stabilize the tethered conformation.

*Figure 7: Summary of HD nanobody binding characteristics. A, binding preferences. B, epitopes. Groups 1 and 5 bind vIII and therefore their epitopes must reside in its segment of EGFR. As with other group 3 nanobodies, the HD25 epitope likely includes the ligand binding site of domain III; HD25 is strongly competitive with EGF and 7D12, which each bind domain III. As with the structurally characterized group 4 nanobody EgB4, HD30 likely binds domains I or II. HD30 does not bind vIII and is strongly competitive with EgB4 which binds across domain I and II.*

Group 4 nanobodies (HD30 and EgB4) and the Group 5 nanobody (HD01) are positively cooperative with EGF, suggesting they favor an active or preactive conformation. They show reciprocal positive cooperativity with one another, further demonstrating they target a shared conformation. Additionally, these nanobodies, along with mAb 806, are directly competitive or negatively cooperative with Groups 1 and 2, which stabilize the closed, inactive conformation. Since Group 2 nanobodies EgA1 and 9G8 are known to bind domain III and Group 4 nanobody EgB4 binds to a non-overlapping site at the domain I-II interface (Fig. 5E), the Group 2 and 4 nanobodies are not directly competitive and must be negatively cooperative with one another. As Group 1 and 2 nanobodies are positively cooperative, these results suggest that Group 4 nanobodies are negatively cooperative, rather than directly competitive, with both Group 1 and Group 2 nanobodies. Overall, Group 4, Group 5, and mAb 806 antibodies appear to stabilize active or pre-active conformations and competition of Groups 1 and 2 with Groups 4 and 5 and mAb 806 appears to result from a competition for binding to mutually exclusive conformations.

This overall model is consistent with subtle differences between Group 1 and 2 antibodies that stabilize the tethered conformation and among Group 4, 5, and 806 antibodies that stabilize active or preactive conformations. Group 1 antibodies are much more sensitive than Group 2 antibodies to GBM mutations. Group 1 but not Group 2 antibodies bind less well to the R84 K and A265 V mutations in domains I and II, whereas G574 V and vIII mutations result in more than a 100-fold decrease in affinity for Group 1 antibodies and ∼2-fold decrease in Group 2 antibody binding. GBM mutations also demonstrate differences among Group 4 and 5 nanobodies and mAb 806. mAb 806 binding is greatly enhanced by domain I-II interface mutants and vIII mutants but not the G574 V mutant. Conversely, HD01 binding is enhanced by G574 V and vIII mutations but not by Domain I-II interface mutants. Binding of the HD30 nanobody in Group 4 but not EgB4 is enhanced by the G574 V mutation. Although binding of the EgB4 antibody in Group 4 is decreased by domain I-II interface mutants, this is likely explained by disruption of this interface, to which it binds. Differences among the conformations stabilized by activating antibodies align with prior molecular dynamic simulations and elastic network models, which suggest that GBM mutations in the Domain I-II interface may stabilize distinct preactive conformations (9).

Preactive EGFR conformations may shift the monomer-dimer EGFR equilibrium towards dimerization. In the tethered structure, G574 is located near the domain II-IV tether, potentially indicating that the G574 V missense mutation destabilizes the tether and drives the EGFR conformational equilibrium toward the untethered/open conformation. In the ligand-bound homodimeric structure (50), the two G574 residues are 6 Å apart in a hydrophobic region of the domain IV-IV interface. A substitution from glycine to valine would further extend this hydrophobic region, potentially stabilizing EGFR homodimers. Therefore, a G574 V mutation could destabilize the tethered conformation while simultaneously stabilizing the unliganded homodimer. In agreement, HD01 preferentially binds vIII, which has been reported to form homodimers on the cell surface (28).

The nanobodies described in this work provide insight into GBM-specific targeting of oncogenic EGFR conformations. The differential selectivity of HD nanobodies and mAb 806 for GBM mutations suggests that mutations in the Domain I-II interface likely stabilize a different conformation than mutations in the domain II-IV interface. Therapeutics that selectively target conformations stabilized by GBM ectodomain mutations may need to independently target conformations stabilized by Domain I-II mutants and Domain IV mutants or overlapping or orthogonal conformations that they both stabilize.

This work presents a comprehensive study on the discovery and characterization of novel conformation-selective anti-EGFR nanobodies. The observed positive and negative cooperativity between nanobodies further elucidates the dynamic equilibrium between active and inactive states of EGFR and the role of oncogenic mutations in shifting this balance. These results demonstrate the utility of conformation-selective nanobodies as both tools for probing EGFR activation mechanisms and as promising candidates for therapeutic development. Future efforts should focus on leveraging these nanobodies for targeted therapies and exploring their potential in combination with emerging treatment modalities, such as antibody-drug conjugates and CAR-T cell therapies, to address EGFR-driven cancers, including GBM.

## Experimental procedures

### Soluble EGFR

EGFR amino acid numbering is for the mature sequence from RefSeq accession NP_001333827.1. Codon-optimized DNA encoding the human EGFR ectodomain (residue L1 to S621) with N-terminal FLAG and 6xhistidine tags (DYKDDDDKGSGHHHHHH) was Gibson assembled with a gene fragment containing human IgG1 Fc (Genbank: AJ294730.1, K105 to K330) into pD2529-CAG vector (ATUM), containing the CD33 secretion peptide (MPLLLLPLLWAGALA), to generate EGFR-Fc fusion constructs. Fc constructs were generated by HiFi assembly of the same N-terminal FLAG-6xhistidine tags and Fc sequence into pD2529-CAG. Plasmid DNA was transfected into Expi293 F cells (Gibco, A14527) using FectoPRO (Polyplus, #101000014) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, 1 L of expi293 F cells were seeded at 1.5e6 cells/ml in Expi293 Expression Media (Gibco). The next day, 0.8 mg of plasmid DNA was added to 100 ml Opti-MEM (Gibco), gently swirled to ensure even mixing, combined with 0.8 ml FectoPRO transfection reagent, and after 10 min at room temperature, added to the cells. The EGFR Fc fusion homodimer ((sEGFR)2-Fc) was generated by transfecting 0.8 mg of EGFR-Fc fusion plasmid DNA per liter and the EGFR-Fc fusion monomer (sEGFR-Fc) was generated by cotransfecting 0.6 mg of EGFR-Fc fusion plasmid DNA with 0.2 mg Fc plasmid DNA per liter (Fig. S1). Glucose (0.4% w/v) and valproic acid (3 mM) were added to the cultures 24 h after transfection.

After 6 days, cells were centrifuged, supernatants filtered using 0.45 μm filters (Sterlitech), and HEPES pH 8 was added to a final concentration of 25 mM HEPES before being combined with 4 ml of Protein A agarose (Gold Biotechnology, P-400–100) per liter of supernatant. Following overnight incubation at 4 °C with gentle rocking, the mixture of Protein A agarose and supernatant was poured over a gravity column to capture the protein-A agarose. The column was then washed with 10 column volumes of Protein A wash buffer (20 mM HEPES pH 7.4 and 150 mM NaCl) and proteins were eluted using 10 column volumes of Protein A elution buffer (100 mM glycine pH 3, 150 mM NaCl) directly into 1 column volume of 2 M HEPES pH 8. Yields averaged ∼30 mg/L for sEGFR-Fc and ∼20 mg/L for (sEGFR)2-Fc.

The Fc region was cleaved from Fc fusion constructs using IdeS protease (Fig. 2). Purified IdeS (1.25 μM) was incubated with a 4-10-fold molar excess of EGFR Fc fusion protein (5 μM −12.5 μM) for 1 h at 37 °C in 50 mM phosphate buffer pH 6.6 and 5 M NaCl. Following IdeS cleavage, (sEGFR)2-hinge and sEGFR-hinge were purified by size-exclusion chromatography (Fig. 2D) using phosphate buffered saline (10 mM phosphate pH 7.4, 137 mM NaCl, 2.7 mM KCl). (sEGFR)2-hinge was gel filtered using an S200 10/300 column and sEGFR-hinge was gel filtered at a slow rate (∼0.05 ml/min) using either a HiLoad S200 16/600 column (Fig. S1B) or two S200 10/300 columns in series (Fig. 2D, right). We used slow rates as faster rates showed less effective separation between sEGFR-hinge and (sEGFR)2-hinge (i.e., more overlap between the two peaks); gel filtration separates proteins based on their diffusion coefficients, and optimal separation depends on diffusion of proteins into the pores of beads reaching equilibrium.

### Nanobodies

#### First campaign

2 × 1010 Saccharomyces cerevisiae cells (10x library diversity) expressing a surface-display library of single-domain camelid antibody VHH domains (nanobodies) (34) were washed and resuspended in yeast selection buffer (20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 0.1% (w/v) bovine serum albumin (BSA), and 5 mM maltose) containing 500 μl anti-FITC-coated magnetic microbeads (Miltenyi) and 1 μM FITC-labeled anti-FLAG M1 mAb (FITC-M1) for 1 h at 4 °C. The yeast cells were then passed through an LD MACS column (Miltenyi) to deplete the library for yeast expressing nanobodies that bind to the magnetic microbeads, anti-FITC mAb, M1 mAb, or FITC. The flowthrough was centrifuged and resuspended in yeast selection buffer containing 1 μM (sEGFR)2-hinge, 1 μM FITC-M1, and 3 μM EGF (Peprotech, AF-100–15). Following a 1 h incubation at room temperature, the yeast cells were centrifuged and resuspended in yeast selection buffer containing 500 μl anti-FITC coated magnetic beads (Miltenyi) and incubated for 20 min at 4 °C with rocking before being passed through an LS MACS column (Miltenyi). The eluates containing yeast-expressing nanobodies targeting ligand-bound (sEGFR)2-hinge were collected, expanded, and used in subsequent rounds.

After MACS, four sequential rounds of fluorescence activated cell sorting (FACS) enriched the library for nanobody binders to (sEGFR)2-hinge. Representative FACS gating strategies are shown in Figure S2. CF647-labeled anti-HA (12CA5) was used for detection of nanobody display on the yeast surface. CF488-labeled (sEGFR)2-hinge and CF405-labeled (sEGFR)2-hinge were alternated in subsequent rounds of FACS to prevent enrichment of fluorophore-specific nanobodies. In FACS 1, we enriched for binders to 500 nM CF488-labeled (sEGFR)2-hinge with or without 3 μM EGF. In FACS 2, the output of FACS1 was divided into three arms: 1) we depleted for binders to Alexa Fluor 488-labeled insect cell membrane polyspecificity reagent (AF488-PSR) (34); 2) we enriched for binders to 150 nM CF405-labeled (sEGFR)2-hinge with 3 μM EGF and depleted for binders to AF488-PSR; and 3) we enriched for binders to 150 nM CF405-labeled (sEGFR)2-hinge and depleted for binders to both AF488-PSR and 150 nM CF488-labeled sEGFR-hinge. In FACS 3, 100 nM FITC-M1 was used to deplete each arm for FITC-M1 binders. In FACS 4, each arm was divided into two subarms: (1) we enriched for binders to 10 nM CF405-labeled (sEGFR)2-hinge with 3 μM transforming growth factor alpha and (2) enriched for binders to 10 nM CF405-labeled (sEGFR)2-hinge and depleted for binders to 10 nM CF488-labeled sEGFR-hinge.

#### Second campaign

Selection was as in campaign one with the following differences. Two separate screens were performed in parallel (as in Fig. 3B). Libraries were enriched either for unliganded (sEGFR)2-hinge or ligand-bound (sEGFR)2-hinge. Using a MACS LD column (Miltenyi), libraries were first depleted for yeast expressing nanobodies that bind to the magnetic microbeads or anti-FITC mAb. The flowthrough was washed and incubated with yeast selection buffer containing 1 μM FITC-labeled (sEGFR)2-hinge with or without 3 μM EGF. Further MACS enrichment was as in selection one.

Following MACS, three sequential FACS steps further enriched the nanobody library for binders to (sEGFR)2-hinge with or without 3 μM EGF. FACS 1 enriched for binders to 200 nM CF-488-labeled (sEGFR)2-hinge; FACS 2 enriched for binders to CF405-labeled 200 nM (sEGFR)2-hinge; and FACS 3 enriched for binders to 100 nM CF-488-labeled (sEGFR)2-hinge. For the libraries enriched for unliganded (sEGFR)2-hinge nanobody binders, FACS 2 depleted for binders to CF488-labeled 200 nM sEGFR-hinge and FACS 3 depleted for binders to 100 nM CF405-labeled sEGFR-hinge. In all selection campaigns, FACS 2 depleted for binders to CF488-PSR (34). FACS 2 and 3 incorporated kinetic selections (35). After incubating yeast cells expressing nanobody with fluorophore-labeled (sEGFR)2-hinge for 1 h at room temperature, cells were washed 2x and resuspended in ice-cold yeast selection buffer containing the same concentration of unlabeled (sEGFR)2-hinge and incubated on ice for 30 min. Cells were then washed 2x with ice-cold yeast selection buffer and yeast cells expressing (sEGFR)2-hinge-selective nanobodies bound to fluorescent (sEGFR)2-hinge with or without EGF were sorted by FACS. Kinetic selections enriched for yeast cells expressing nanobodies with slow off-rates, increasing the likelihood of enriching for high affinity nanobody binders.

#### Post-immune nanobody library

An adult male alpaca (Vicugna pacos) was immunized as described (51). Four immunizations were administered at 2-week intervals. For each immunization, 14 different proteins including (sEGFR)2-hinge (100 μl of each at 1 mg/ml) were mixed. The 1.4 ml solution was mixed with alum adjuvant (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Two weeks after the final immunization, 60 to 80 ml of blood was collected and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated by Ficoll gradient separation (∼107 cells). RNA was isolated from PBMCs using an RNeasy Micro Kit (Qiagen) and was reverse transcribed to cDNA using the SuperScript II Reverse Transcriptase Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturers’ protocols. Three reverse transcriptions were performed in parallel using the following primer pairings: (1) random hexamers and oligo dT primers; (2) random hexamers and primers specific to alpaca IgG2; and (3) random hexamers and primers specific to alpaca IgG3 (Table S3). cDNA was generated according to previously established methods (52). First-strand cDNA was pooled and used as a template in two parallel PCR reactions to amplify the IgG2 and IgG3 variable domain genes with hinge region-specific primers (Table S3). After gel purification, the resulting PCR products served as templates for two final PCRs, performed in parallel for IgG2 and IgG3 nanobody genes.

pCTcon2 vector (Addgene, Plasmid # 41843) was cleaved with NheI and BamHI endonucleases (New England Biolabs). Linearized pCTcon2 vector and PCR amplicons containing nanobody genes were gel purified and ethanol precipitated. Linearized vector (50 μg) and nanobody PCR product (250 μg) were transformed into S. cerevisiae (EBY100 strain) by electroporation using a BTX high-throughput square wave electroporator (53) to allow homologous recombination in yeast. After a 45 min incubation, the size of the library (2 x 108 yeast clones) was determined by plating serial dilutions on YPD plates. The transformed library was expanded for 2 days in -Trp selection media (20 mM citrate buffer pH 4.5, 0.38% (w/v) -Trp dropout media (US Biological, D9531), 0.67% (w/v) yeast nitrogen base (HiMedia, M878), 2% (w/v) glucose and 1% (v/v) Penicillin-Streptomycin (Gibco, 15,140,122)) before being aliquoted and frozen in 10% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) using a Mr Frosty (Thermo Scientific) according to manufacturer’s instructions.

#### Third selection campaign

Third selections were as second selections except using the post-immune nanobody library. FITC-labeled anti C-Myc polyclonal chicken antibody (ICL lab; CMYC-45F) was used for detection of nanobody display on the yeast surface. FACS 1 and 3 enriched for CF647-labeled (sEGFR)2-hinge. For the libraries enriched for unliganded (sEGFR)2-hinge nanobody binders, FACS 2 depleted for binders to CF647-labeled sEGFR-hinge. All sEGFR-hinge, (sEGFR)2-hinge, and EGF concentrations were identical to second selections. PSR was not used.

#### Determining nanobody sequences

After each round of MACS and FACS, plasmid DNA was isolated (Zymo Research, D2997) from yeast nanobody libraries. At the end of each selection campaign, plasmid DNA was used as template in PCRs to amplify nanobody genes from each sample and add sample-specific 6-bp DNA barcodes. The resultant amplicons were pooled and subjected to multiplexed sequencing using the Illumina platform. Sequences were demultiplexed to separate reads by their sample-specific barcodes and analyzed according to (34). The most enriched nanobody sequences at the end of each campaign, as determined by highest read counts in Illumina sequencing, were expressed as soluble nanobodies.

In parallel to illumina sequencing, we stained clonal yeast populations to identify individual nanobodies that bind (sEGFR)2-hinge (31). Following selection campaigns, yeast nanobody libraries enriched for (sEGFR)2-hinge binders were serial diluted on YPD plates. Single colonies were picked and grown as clonal populations. Nanobody expression was induced with galactose-containing media. Yeast were washed and resuspended in yeast selection buffer containing fluorescently labeled (sEGFR)2-hinge at 10 nM (FACS 1) or 100 nM (FACS 2 and 3) in the presence and absence of 3 μM EGF. Following 2x washes and resuspension in yeast selection buffer, binding to (sEGFR)2-hinge was assessed by flow cytometry using a FACSCanto (BD Biosciences). Gating strategies were as in Figure S2B. For clonal yeast populations expressing nanobodies that bound (sEGFR)2-hinge, DNA was extracted, their nanobody genes PCR amplified, and their sequences determined by Sanger sequencing.

#### Expressing soluble nanobodies

Nanobodies were generated according to (34). Nanobody genes were cloned into pET26b, which includes the N-terminal pelB signal peptide (MKYLLPTAAAGLLLLAAQPAMA) for periplasmic expression and C-terminal V5 and 6x histidine tags (GKPIPNPLLGLDSTLEHHHHHH). Following transformation into E. coli BL21 (DE3) and kanamycin selection, bacteria were grown in Terrific Broth (89 mM phosphate buffer pH 7.6, 1.2% tryptone, 2.4% yeast extract) with 4% (v/v) glycerol at 37 °C until an OD600 of 1.5 to 2 was reached. The incubator was reduced to 17 °C for 1 h then cultures were induced with 200 μM Isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) (Gold Biotechnology, I2481 C). Induction was performed at 17 °C for 16 to 24 h. Cells were then centrifuged and resuspended in 50 ml of room temperature buffer containing 0.5 M sucrose, 0.2 M Tris pH 8, and 0.5 mM EDTA. After stirring for 30 min, 100 ml of ice-cold water containing 5 mM MgCl2 and 250 units benzonase (Millipore) was added to release the periplasmic nanobody through osmotic shock. After an additional 1 h of stirring, cells were pelleted, and the lysate was adjusted to a final concentration of 150 mM NaCl. Lysate was then applied to Roche cOmplete His-Tag Purification Resin gravity columns and purified according to manufacturer’s protocol followed by protein-A purification (Gold Biotechnology, P-400–100) as previously described (34). Finally, purified nanobodies were applied to an S75 size-exclusion chromatography column using HEPES Buffered saline (20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, and 10% (v/v) glycerol), concentrated, flash frozen, and stored at −80 °C.

### Monoclonal antibodies

anti-EGFR LA22 (ATCC, HB-10342), 4E11 anti-FLAG M1 (ATCC, HB-9259), and 12CA5 anti-HA (donated by Andrew Kruse lab) hybridomas were expanded to 106 cell/ml in 1 L total volume using Cell mAb Media (Gibco, 220,513) supplemented with 10 mM L-glutamine. Cells were transferred to roller culture bottles and incubated with continuous rolling until they reached 50% viability. Cells were then centrifuged, supernatant was harvested, and antibodies were purified by protein A purification as described in “soluble EGFR” section.

mAb 806 was expressed recombinantly. Heavy and light chain sequences (PDB: 3G5X) were codon optimized, and Gibson assembled into the pD2529-CAG vector (ATUM). Signal peptides were METDTLLLWVLLLWVPGSTG for light chain and MDWTWRILFLVAAATGAHS for heavy chain. A mixture of light chain (533 μg) and heavy chain (266 μg) plasmid DNA (2:1 ratio) was transfected into Expi293 F cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using FectoPRO (Polyplus, #101000014) as outlined in the “Soluble EGFR” section. After 6 days, the supernatant was harvested, and antibodies were purified by protein A purification as described in the “soluble EGFR” section.

All antibodies were fluorescently labeled according to (54).

### Full-length EGFR on the cell surface

Sequences encoding full-length WT EGFR and EGFR GBM mutants were cloned into the ET-1 expression vector (55). Final plasmid constructs contained the pIRES sequence flanked 5′ by EGFR and 3′ by EGFP. Expi293 F cells were transiently transfected using jetPrime reagent (Polyplus) according to the manufacturer’s instructions and assayed 24 h later. EGFR GBM mutants showed decreased expression compared to WT EGFR; mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) of stained mutants was normalized relative to CF647-labeled mAb LA22 (stained at 100 nM), which recognizes a linear epitope in domain III (42). Expi293 F cells were tested to be mycoplasma free.

Ba/F3 cells stably transfected with WT EGFR were generated previously in our lab (50) and were tested to be mycoplasma free.

#### Indirect flow cytometry

All washes were performed in wash buffer (HBSS with 1% (w/v) BSA), and all incubations and flow cytometry measurements were performed in FACS buffer (L-15 media (Gibco) with 1% (w/v) BSA). Ba/F3 stable transfectants expressing WT EGFR or transiently transfected EGFR WT and GBM mutants (106 cells/ml) were washed and resuspended in FACS buffer containing the indicated concentration of antibodies or nanobodies. Ba/F3 cells expressing WT EGFR were incubated with antibodies or nanobodies for 1 h with rocking at room temperature; Expi293 F cells transiently transfected with WT EGFR or mutant EGFR were incubated with rocking for 3 to 4 h at 4 °C to prevent EGFR internalization. Following primary incubation, cells were washed 3x and resuspended in FACS buffer containing Alexa Fluor 647-labeled anti-V5 (1:1000) secondary mAb (Invitrogen, 451,098) for 20 min at 4 °C. Cells were then washed 2x, resuspended in FACS buffer, and immediately subjected to flow cytometry using a FACSCanto (BD Biosciences).

In assays with Ba/F3 stable transfectants and Expi293 F transient transfectants, the first gate was FSC-A versus SSC-A to select for live cells and the second gate was FSC-A versus FSC-H to select for single cells. For Expi293 F cells, a third additional gate was set for all cells expressing co-transfected EGFP. Alexa Fluor 647-labeled anti-V5 staining was measured on the single-cell population for Ba/F3 cells and measured on the EGFP-positive population for Expi293 F cells. Background MFI was quantified for Ba/F3 WT EGFR stable transfectants by measuring binding (MFI) to untransfected parental Ba/F3 cells, which do not express WT EGFR, and was quantified for transiently transfected cells by measuring binding (MFI) to cells transfected with empty vector; background staining was performed at the same concentration as the primary antibodies or nanobodies. Background subtracted MFI values are reported as specific MFI (sMFI).

### Competition assays (cell-surface binning)

Ba/F3 stable transfectants expressing WT EGFR (106 cells/ml) were washed with ice-cold HBSS containing 1% BSA. Cells were resuspended in L-15 media (Gibco) containing 1% (w/v) BSA, and CF647-labeled nanobody, mAb, or EGF at their EC50 concentrations, and unlabeled nanobody, mAb, or EGF at 100x their EC50 concentrations, and incubated for 3 to 4 h with rocking at 4 °C to prevent EGFR internalization. All antibodies and EGF were fluorescently labeled according to (54). Following incubation, fluorescence intensity was measured by flow cytometry using a FACSCanto (BD Biosciences). Background MFI was quantified by CF647-labeled binder binding to parental Ba/F3 cells—which do not endogenously express EGFR—in the absence of competitor. Measurements were performed in triplicate. Values in Figure 5A were generated using the following equation:

$$ sMFI cooperativity = sMFI with competitor s MFI no competitor = MFI with competitor − MFI background MFI no competitor − MFI background $$

The dendrogram was created in R(47) using the dist method in hclust, plotted using ggplot2 (56), and its visual aspects were modified using the dendextend package (57). The community network plot was generated in R using the igraph package (58), grouped using the Walktrap community finding algorithm (48), and visually modified using the tidygraph package (59). Community network plots show only competition (i.e., negative cooperativity) values that are statistically significant: In detail, sMFIcooperativity values less than 0.9 that had statistically significant difference between sMFIwith competitor and sMFIno competitor using Bonferroni-corrected unpaired t-tests.

### Treatment with allosteric inhibitors

Gefitinib (US Biological, 184,475) and lapatinib (MedChemExpress, GW572016) stocks were dissolved in DMSO at 1000x their working concentrations and stored at −80 °C. Ba/F3 cells stably transfected with WT EGFR were incubated with 50 μM gefitinib, 10 μM lapatinib, or DMSO for 30 min at 37 °C. Wash buffer (HBSS with 1% (w/v) BSA) and FACS buffer (L-15 media with 1% (w/v) BSA) had the indicated concentrations of gefitinib, lapatinib, or DMSO throughout the assay. Cells were washed 2x and resuspended in FACS buffer containing the designated nanobody at its EC05 concentration. Following 1 h incubation at 4 °C with rocking, cells were washed 3x with wash buffer and resuspended in FACS buffer containing Alexa Fluor 647-labeled anti-V5 (1:1000) secondary mAb for 20 min at 4 °C. Cells were washed 2x, resuspended in FACS buffer, and immediately subjected to flow cytometry using a FACSCanto (BD Biosciences). All buffers in the assay contained the designated amount of inhibitor. Cells treated with gefitinib and lapatinib showed decreased EGFR expression. Expression was normalized using LA22 mAb according to ‘Full-length EGFR on the cell surface’ section.

### Isothermal titration calorimetry

All isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) experiments were performed using a MicroCal ITC200 instrument at 20 °C. Purified proteins were buffer exchanged into a buffer containing 50 mM phosphate (pH 6.8) and 150 mM NaCl. The concentration of ligand in the syringe ranged from 50 μM to 250 μM and the concentration of sEGFR-Fc or (sEGFR)2-Fc in the cell ranged from 10 μM – 30 μM. Data were analyzed using a single-site binding model in the Origin software package to calculate ΔH, ΔS, KD, and n values.
